questions.q: Why does a network break data into small pieces instead of sending it as one continuous stream?
options: It doesn't — modern networks always send data as one unbroken stream
So many conversations can share a link fairly, and only a lost piece needs to be resent, not the whole transmission
Small pieces are required by law in most countries
Because routers cannot process more than one bit at a time
questions.explain: Breaking data into pieces lets a shared link interleave many conversations and means only the lost or corrupted piece has to be retransmitted.

questions.q: What is the correct order, from Layer 4 down to Layer 2, that a unit of data is called as it's prepared for transmission?
options: Packet, then segment, then frame
Frame, then packet, then segment
Segment, then packet, then frame
Bit, then frame, then packet
questions.explain: Transport (Layer 4) produces a segment, Network (Layer 3) wraps it into a packet, and Data Link (Layer 2) wraps that into a frame.

questions.q: What does "encapsulation" mean in the context of the OSI model?
options: Compressing data to make it smaller before sending it
Each layer wrapping the layer above it in its own header as data moves down the stack
Encrypting data so it can't be read in transit
Converting analog signals to digital signals
questions.explain: Encapsulation is each layer adding its own header (and sometimes trailer) around the data handed down from the layer above.

questions.q: A technician says "it's a Layer 1 problem." What does that most likely mean?
options: The DNS server is misconfigured
The application protocol itself is broken
There's a literal physical issue — a cable, port, or radio link
A firewall rule is blocking the wrong port
questions.explain: Layer 1 is the Physical layer — cables, radio signals, light pulses. A Layer 1 problem means nothing above it can work until the physical link itself is fixed.

questions.q: Why do network professionals typically troubleshoot bottom-up, starting at Layer 1, instead of starting with the application?
options: Because the application layer is always the last thing installed
Because nothing above a broken lower layer can work no matter how correct it is, so confirming the physical link first avoids wasted effort
Because Layer 1 issues are the rarest and easiest to rule out
There's no real reason — it's just a tradition with no practical benefit
questions.explain: If a lower layer is broken, every layer above it is broken too, regardless of how correctly it's configured — so ruling out the physical link first saves time.
